justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what I infer was a baseline price around $105–106. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of $105.8 suggests near-term mean reversion or slight continuation of recent momentum, with relatively little expected movement over a single session. At the one-week horizon, the slight uptick to $106.5 incorporates a mild positive drift assumption, acknowledging that markets tend to drift modestly upward over short horizons in the absence of strong contrary signals. The one-month estimate of $107.0 extends this logic further, implying a slow, gradual appreciation consistent with a low-volatility trending environment. All three point estimates are essentially anchored near the current price, reflecting limited conviction about directional movement.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty. At one day, the $103.2–$108.4 range captures typical intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, the interval broadens to $100.5–$112.5, acknowledging that unexpected macro data, earnings releases, or technical breakdowns could shift sentiment meaningfully. At one month, the $96.0–$118.0 range is quite wide, reflecting cumulative uncertainty from multiple weeks of potential news flow, policy changes, and market regime shifts.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as a surprise central bank policy decision, geopolitical escalation, or a significant earnings miss or beat from a systemically important company. A liquidity crisis or flash crash scenario could easily breach the lower bound even at the one-day horizon, while a short squeeze or risk-on rally driven by unexpectedly strong economic data could push prices above the upper bounds. These tail events, by definition, are not fully captured in the stated intervals since I am only expressing 90% confidence.

It is also worth noting that these forecasts were generated without real-time data, so if the underlying asset had already moved significantly prior to the forecast being made, the stated intervals may be systematically off-center. Model uncertainty itself — meaning uncertainty about which forecasting framework is most appropriate — adds an additional layer of risk that is not fully embedded in the stated confidence intervals, making the true uncertainty somewhat wider than what the numbers alone suggest.
